title: Her sister Josephine and bringing her mother to Chicago
summary: Josephine died at 17; Hunter brought her mother to Chicago, who never objected to show business and taught her to always be a lady.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Whatever happened to Josephine, your sister?
Josephine? Well, Josephine was only 17 years old when she died. She came to Chicago to see my mother. And that was the first time I had seen her since she was a little tiny girl.
I brought her up to Chicago.

Brought my mother soon as I got a good job. Soon as I got a job where I knew I was making permanent money, I got an apartment and put my mother in it. Sure, she came right on from Memphis to Chicago. Came from Memphis to Chicago, and said she didn't like Chicago, and I had to send her back to Memphis. My money.
So then she finally made up her mind, she come to Chicago and stayed. And then I got her this apartment. She was with me all along, ever since.
How did she feel about show business? Did she look down on it, as sort of not a very --
No, my mother was a very wellbred woman, and a woman of -- you know, she --
D.C. wasn't -- you met D.C. didn't you?

No, D.C. didn't want no show business for Lil. Uh-uh. But my mother was a different type person. My mother -- she didn't criticize show business. And she didn't try to keep me out of show business. As long as I was a good girl, she always told me, be a lady. Always be a lady. That was beaten in my head all my life. Respect yourself, and you'll be respected. That was always my training, see. And so my mother, when my mother came to Chicago -- came to Memphis -- I mean, came from Memphis to Chicago, she contented herself, but she was like I am. She was a lone wolf, she'd never visit
people. Never visited anybody. She stayed in the house by herself. But she had everything that a poor girl could give her mother, because I saw to that, you know.
